stem: A company builds AI agents with different frameworks. Each agent needs access to the same internal systems, such as the CRM, a ticketing tool and a document store. Today every team writes its own custom integration for every agent.
prompt: Which standard is designed to let agents connect to external tools and data sources through a common interface?

options.text: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
options.why: SMTP sends email between servers and has nothing to do with connecting agents to tools.

options.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
options.why: MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications discover and call tools and access data through MCP servers, so one integration can serve many agents.

options.text: BLEU
options.why: BLEU is a metric for evaluating machine translation quality, not an integration standard.

options.text: Structured Query Language (SQL)
options.why: SQL queries relational databases. It does not standardize how AI agents discover and call arbitrary tools.

explanation.answer: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications and agents to external systems. MCP servers expose tools, resources and prompts; MCP clients inside agents discover and use them. Building an MCP server once lets any MCP-compatible agent use that system.
explanation.concept: On AWS, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway can turn existing APIs and AWS Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools, and frameworks such as Strands Agents can consume MCP servers.
explanation.examTip: Standard way for agents to connect to tools and data = MCP.

stem: A developer is learning the Model Context Protocol and wants to understand its basic architecture.
prompt: Which description of MCP is MOST accurate?

options.text: A standard API that every model provider implements for model calls
options.why: MCP does not standardize how models are invoked; it standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools and data.

options.text: A protocol that lets agents delegate tasks to other agents
options.why: Agent-to-agent delegation is addressed by agent-to-agent protocols. MCP connects AI applications to tools, resources and prompts.

options.text: Clients in AI apps connect to servers exposing tools, resources and prompts
options.why: MCP is client-server: the application's MCP clients connect to MCP servers that advertise capabilities the model can use.

options.text: A format for documenting a model's training data and limits
options.why: That describes model cards. MCP is a runtime integration protocol.

explanation.answer: MCP uses a client-server model. The AI application (host) runs MCP clients that connect to MCP servers. Servers advertise capabilities, chiefly tools (actions the model can invoke), resources (data it can read) and prompts (reusable templates), and the model decides when to use them.
explanation.concept: Standardizing integrations reduces duplicate work and makes tools portable across agent frameworks. Security still matters: servers should enforce authentication, authorization and least privilege.
explanation.examTip: MCP = clients in the AI app, servers exposing tools, resources and prompts.

stem: A user asks an AI assistant, "What is the current status of my order 48213?" The underlying model was trained months ago and has no access to live order data.
prompt: Which agentic capability allows the assistant to answer correctly?

options.text: RAG over the company's order documentation
options.why: Documentation describes how orders work; it does not contain the live status of order 48213.

options.text: Fine-tuning the model on recent order histories
options.why: Training data is frozen at training time and cannot reflect the current status of a specific order.

options.text: Long-term memory of the user's past orders
options.why: Memory holds what was said before, not the order's current status in the order system.

options.text: Tool use: calling an order-status API for live data
options.why: Tool use lets the model request an API call and use the live result in its answer.

explanation.answer: Tool use (also called function calling) lets a model decide to call external functions or APIs with structured parameters. The application executes the call and returns the result, which the model uses to answer. This gives models access to live data and the ability to take actions.
explanation.concept: Tools are described to the model with names, descriptions and input schemas. Good tool descriptions and least-privilege permissions are essential for reliable, safe agents.
explanation.examTip: Model needs live data or must act on a system = tool use / function calling.

references.title: Automate tasks with Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: An insurance company designs an AI system for claims. One agent receives each claim, breaks the work into parts, and delegates to specialized agents for policy lookup, damage assessment and fraud screening. It then combines their results into a final recommendation.
prompt: Which multi-agent pattern does this describe?

options.text: Supervisor (orchestrator) with specialist sub-agents
options.why: One coordinating agent decomposes the task, delegates to specialists and combines their results.

options.text: Sequential pipeline of agents in a fixed order
options.why: In a pipeline each agent passes output to the next; here one agent delegates and then aggregates.

options.text: Parallel fan-out with no coordinating agent
options.why: The scenario has a coordinating agent that breaks down the work and assembles the final recommendation.

options.text: Decentralized peer-to-peer handoffs between agents
options.why: In peer handoffs agents pass control to each other directly; here a single agent controls delegation.

explanation.answer: In the supervisor (orchestrator-worker) pattern, a coordinating agent plans the work, delegates subtasks to specialized agents and synthesizes their results. Specialization keeps each agent's instructions and tools focused, which improves reliability.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Agents supports multi-agent collaboration with a supervisor agent, and frameworks such as Strands Agents support patterns including agents-as-tools, swarms, graphs and workflows.
explanation.examTip: One agent coordinates and delegates to specialists = supervisor pattern.

references.title: Multi-agent collaboration in Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: A content team builds a system in which a research agent gathers facts, then passes its notes to a writing agent, which passes a draft to an editing agent, which produces the final article. Each agent always runs in the same order.
prompt: Which multi-agent pattern is this?

options.text: Reinforcement learning from human feedback
options.why: RLHF is a model training method, not a pattern for coordinating agents at runtime.

options.text: Sequential (pipeline) pattern
options.why: Each agent processes the previous agent's output in a fixed order, which is a sequential pipeline.

options.text: Retrieval augmented generation
options.why: RAG supplies retrieved documents to a model. It does not describe agents handing work to each other.

options.text: Parallel fan-out pattern
options.why: In a parallel pattern, agents work at the same time on separate parts. Here each step waits for the previous one.

explanation.answer: In the sequential (pipeline or workflow) pattern, agents run in a predefined order, each consuming the previous agent's output. It is predictable and easy to debug, which suits processes with clear stages.
explanation.concept: Other patterns: parallel (independent subtasks at the same time, then merge), supervisor/orchestrator (dynamic delegation), and peer or swarm (agents hand off to each other dynamically). Choose based on how predictable the workflow is.
explanation.examTip: Fixed order, output passed along = sequential pattern.

stem: A due-diligence system must analyze a company's financial statements, legal filings and news coverage. The three analyses are independent of each other, and the team wants results as quickly as possible before a final agent merges them.
prompt: Which pattern is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Run the three analyses one after another in a strict sequence
options.why: Running independent tasks in sequence wastes time because no task depends on another's output.

options.text: Use a single prompt with no tools
options.why: A single prompt would mix three large analyses and lose the benefits of specialization and concurrency.

options.text: Parallel (fan-out/fan-in): run the three specialist agents at the same time, then aggregate
options.why: Independent subtasks can run concurrently, reducing total time, and a final step merges the results.

options.text: Fine-tune one model per document type before every request
options.why: Fine-tuning per request is slow and costly and is not an orchestration pattern.

explanation.answer: The parallel (fan-out/fan-in or scatter-gather) pattern runs independent subtasks concurrently and then aggregates the results. It reduces latency when subtasks do not depend on each other.
explanation.concept: Workflow orchestration chooses between sequential, parallel, conditional and dynamic (agent-decided) execution depending on dependencies between steps.
explanation.examTip: Independent subtasks + speed = parallel fan-out, then merge.

stem: A travel assistant should remember what the user said earlier in the current conversation, and also remember across separate conversations that the user prefers aisle seats and vegetarian meals.
prompt: Which memory design meets these needs?

options.text: Rely on the context window and keep conversations open for weeks
options.why: A context window does not persist across separate conversations, and very long contexts become slow and costly.

options.text: Store preferences in the system prompt shared by all users
options.why: A shared system prompt would apply one user's preferences to everyone and expose them to other users.

options.text: Fine-tune the model whenever a user states a preference
options.why: Retraining per user preference is slow, expensive and impractical.

options.text: Session memory for the conversation plus long-term preference memory
options.why: Short-term memory keeps the current dialogue coherent; long-term memory persists extracted preferences for future sessions.

explanation.answer: Agents typically use two kinds of memory. Short-term memory holds the current session's conversation and state. Long-term memory stores durable information, such as preferences, facts and summaries, extracted from interactions and retrieved in later sessions.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory provides managed short-term and long-term memory for agents. Memory should respect privacy: store only what is needed and allow deletion.
explanation.examTip: Within a conversation = short-term memory. Across conversations = long-term memory.

stem: An agent receives the task "Find the three cheapest flights to Denver next Friday and email the options to my manager." It thinks about what to do, calls a flight-search tool, examines the results, decides it needs the manager's address, calls a directory tool, and then calls an email tool.
prompt: Which concept BEST describes this behavior?

options.text: A reason-and-act loop: think, call a tool, observe, repeat
options.why: The agent alternates between reasoning and tool calls, using each result to decide the next step (ReAct).

options.text: A sequential multi-agent pipeline with fixed steps
options.why: One agent is acting here, and the steps were chosen dynamically from what it observed, not fixed in advance.

options.text: Chain-of-thought prompting within a single response
options.why: Chain-of-thought reasons before one answer; it does not call tools and react to their results.

options.text: A predefined Bedrock Flow with three fixed nodes
options.why: In a flow the steps are defined in advance; here the agent decided it needed the directory lookup only after seeing results.

explanation.answer: Agents commonly run an iterative loop: the model reasons about the goal and current state, chooses an action (a tool call), observes the result, and repeats until it can finish. This approach is often called ReAct (reason + act).
explanation.concept: The loop needs limits, such as a maximum number of steps, timeouts and cost controls, plus observability to trace each reasoning step and tool call.
explanation.examTip: Think → act (tool) → observe → repeat = agent reasoning loop.

stem: A bank's loan process must always run identity verification, then a credit check, then a compliance review, in that exact order with full auditability. An FM is used only to summarize documents within certain steps.
prompt: Which orchestration approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Use a diffusion model to plan the steps
options.why: Diffusion models generate images and cannot orchestrate business processes.

options.text: A deterministic, predefined workflow that calls the FM only inside specific steps
options.why: When steps and order are mandatory, a predefined workflow guarantees the sequence and auditability while still using the FM where it adds value.

options.text: Skip orchestration and ask users to run each step manually
options.why: Manual steps lose automation and consistency and increase the risk of skipped checks.

options.text: Let a fully autonomous agent decide which steps to run and in what order on each request
options.why: Fully autonomous ordering adds unpredictability. Regulated processes with fixed required steps need deterministic control.

explanation.answer: Workflow orchestration can be deterministic (steps and order defined in advance) or dynamic (an agent chooses steps). For regulated processes with required steps and audit needs, a predefined workflow that embeds FM calls at specific points provides control and predictability.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Flows and AWS Step Functions orchestrate predefined workflows that include model calls. Use autonomous agents where flexibility is valuable and risk is manageable.
explanation.examTip: Mandatory steps in a fixed order = deterministic workflow, not a free-roaming agent.

stem: A procurement agent can create purchase orders. The company wants the agent to work autonomously for small purchases but never commit to purchases above $10,000 without a person's approval.
prompt: Which design BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Instruct the agent not to approve purchases above $10,000
options.why: An instruction is soft guidance that the model may not always follow; the limit needs enforcement in the workflow.

options.text: Review all purchase orders in a weekly audit
options.why: A weekly audit happens after large purchases are already committed.

options.text: Require human approval in the workflow above the threshold
options.why: A required approval step keeps small purchases autonomous while preventing large commitments without a person.

options.text: Remove the tool and have staff create every order
options.why: This removes the automation the company wants for small purchases.

explanation.answer: Agents that take consequential actions should include human-in-the-loop controls, such as user confirmation or approval workflows, for high-risk actions. Combined with least-privilege permissions and policy limits, this balances automation with safety.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock Agents supports user confirmation before invoking actions, and Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can enforce rules about which tools agents may call and with what parameters.
explanation.examTip: High-impact agent action = require human approval.

references.title: Automate tasks with Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: In a customer-service system, a triage agent hands a conversation directly to a billing agent, which may in turn hand it to a technical agent if it discovers a device problem. No single coordinator controls every handoff.
prompt: Which multi-agent communication pattern is this?

options.text: Centralized supervisor pattern
options.why: In a supervisor pattern one coordinator routes all work; here agents hand off to each other directly.

options.text: Sequential pipeline pattern
options.why: A pipeline runs agents in a fixed order; here the next agent depends on what each agent discovers.

options.text: Parallel fan-out and fan-in pattern
options.why: Fan-out runs agents at the same time and merges results; here one agent hands the conversation to the next.

options.text: Decentralized peer-to-peer handoffs (swarm-style)
options.why: Agents pass control to one another based on what they find, with no central coordinator.

explanation.answer: Multi-agent communication can be centralized (a supervisor routes all work) or decentralized (agents hand off to peers directly, as in swarm or network patterns). Decentralized handoffs are flexible but harder to predict and trace.
explanation.concept: Whatever the pattern, shared context and clear handoff protocols matter, and observability is essential to trace which agent did what.
explanation.examTip: Central coordinator = supervisor. Agents hand off to each other = peer / swarm.

stem: An architect lists the building blocks of a typical AI agent.
prompt: Which components are core parts of an AI agent? (Select THREE.)

options.text: A GPU cluster that the agent must re-train on each request
options.why: Agents do not retrain the model per request. They use a trained model at inference time.

options.text: A diffusion model for every agent
options.why: Diffusion models generate images. They are not a required part of an agent.

options.text: Memory that keeps conversation state and useful context
options.why: Memory lets the agent stay coherent within a session and recall relevant information across sessions.

options.text: Tools or APIs the agent can call to act and get information
options.why: Tools let the agent access live data and take actions in external systems.

options.text: A foundation model that reasons and plans
options.why: The FM interprets goals, plans steps and decides which actions to take.

explanation.answer: A typical AI agent combines a foundation model (reasoning and planning), instructions describing its role, tools (APIs, functions, knowledge bases, MCP servers) for acting and retrieving information, memory, and an orchestration loop that ties them together.
explanation.concept: Production agents also need identity and access controls, guardrails, observability and evaluation.
explanation.examTip: Agent = model + instructions + tools + memory + orchestration loop.

stem: A manager asks why the team is calling its new system an "agent" rather than a chatbot.
prompt: Which feature MOST distinguishes an AI agent from a simple chatbot?

options.text: It plans steps and takes actions in other systems through tools
options.why: Agents go beyond answering: they plan multi-step work and act through tools and APIs to reach goals.

options.text: It uses a larger foundation model than a chatbot does
options.why: Agents and chatbots can use the same models; model size is not what makes something an agent.

options.text: It remembers earlier messages in the conversation
options.why: Ordinary chatbots also keep conversation history, so this does not distinguish an agent.

options.text: It can answer questions from company documents
options.why: A RAG chatbot can do this too; answering from documents is not taking actions.

explanation.answer: A chatbot primarily converses and answers questions. An AI agent pursues goals: it plans steps, uses tools to retrieve information and perform actions, and adapts based on results, with varying degrees of autonomy.
explanation.concept: Autonomy should match risk. Low-risk tasks can be fully automated, while high-impact actions should require human approval.
explanation.examTip: Agent = takes actions toward a goal; chatbot = mainly talks.

stem: A platform team plans to expose its internal inventory system as an MCP server.
prompt: What is the MAIN benefit of this approach?

options.text: The inventory data is copied into each agent's knowledge base
options.why: MCP gives agents live access to tools; it does not copy data into each agent.

options.text: Any MCP-compatible agent can use the tools without custom integration
options.why: A standard interface means one server works with many clients and frameworks.

options.text: MCP handles security, so the server needs no access controls
options.why: MCP servers still need authentication, authorization and least privilege.

options.text: Agents can read the inventory without any network calls
options.why: Agents call the MCP server over the network or a local transport; data is not embedded in the agent.

explanation.answer: MCP replaces many one-off integrations with one standard interface. Once a system is exposed as an MCP server, any compatible agent, assistant or IDE can list its tools and call them, which speeds up development and keeps integrations consistent.
explanation.concept: Treat MCP servers like any API: apply authentication, least-privilege authorization, input validation and logging.
explanation.examTip: Build once, use from many agents = MCP's main benefit.

stem: A long-running agent conversation has grown to hundreds of turns. Responses are slowing down, costs are rising, and older details are crowding out the current task.
prompt: Which memory management technique BEST addresses this?

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window
options.why: More room delays the problem but keeps growing cost and latency, and old turns still crowd out the task.

options.text: Lower max tokens so each response is shorter
options.why: The growth is in the input history, not the responses.

options.text: Summarize older turns and retrieve stored facts only when relevant
options.why: Compressing history and retrieving key facts on demand keeps context small and focused while preserving what matters.

options.text: Start a new session every 20 turns and drop the history
options.why: Discarding history loses details the task may still need.

explanation.answer: Memory management for agents includes summarizing older conversation turns, extracting durable facts into long-term memory, and retrieving only relevant memories into the context. This controls token usage, latency and cost while keeping the agent focused.
explanation.concept: This is a context engineering practice. Managed services such as AgentCore Memory can extract and retrieve memories automatically.
explanation.examTip: Long conversations → summarize and retrieve selectively, don't append forever.

stem: A team's single agent has 40 tools and very long instructions covering sales, support and billing. It often picks the wrong tool.
prompt: Why might splitting it into a multi-agent system help?

options.text: Several agents usually cost less, because each uses fewer tokens
options.why: More agents can mean more model calls, so cost may rise. The benefit is accuracy and maintainability.

options.text: One model can then call all 40 tools in parallel
options.why: The issue is choosing the right tool, not running tools in parallel.

options.text: Tools no longer need detailed descriptions
options.why: Each specialist still relies on clear tool descriptions to choose correctly.

options.text: Each specialist gets focused instructions and a few relevant tools
options.why: Narrower scope per agent gives the model fewer, clearer choices and better instructions, which improves tool selection.

explanation.answer: Multi-agent systems break complex applications into specialized agents, each with focused instructions, tools and knowledge. This improves accuracy and maintainability, and lets teams develop and update agents independently.
explanation.concept: Trade-offs: more coordination overhead, more model calls and more complex debugging. Use multiple agents when complexity justifies it.
explanation.examTip: Too many tools and responsibilities in one agent → split into specialists.

references.title: Multi-agent collaboration in Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: An HR agent must answer policy questions from the employee handbook and also submit vacation requests to the HR system.
prompt: How should the agent be equipped for both tasks?

options.text: A knowledge base for the handbook and an action for the HR API
options.why: The knowledge base grounds policy answers in the handbook, and the action lets the agent submit requests.

options.text: Two knowledge bases: one for the handbook, one for vacation data
options.why: Knowledge bases retrieve information; they cannot submit vacation requests to the HR system.

options.text: An action for the HR API, with the handbook pasted into instructions
options.why: Pasting the whole handbook wastes tokens on every request and goes stale when policies change.

options.text: A model fine-tuned on the handbook with a guardrail for requests
options.why: Fine-tuning does not let the agent submit requests, and a guardrail filters content rather than calling the API.

explanation.answer: Agents combine knowledge and actions. Knowledge bases (RAG) provide grounded information from documents, while action groups or tools call APIs to perform tasks. Amazon Bedrock Agents supports both knowledge bases and action groups.
explanation.concept: Separating knowledge (read) from actions (write) also helps apply different permissions and guardrails to each.
explanation.examTip: Answer from documents = knowledge base. Do something in a system = tool / action.

references.title: Automate tasks with Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: An agent sometimes produces wrong results, and the team cannot tell whether the problem is in the model's reasoning, a tool returning bad data, or a step being skipped.
prompt: Which capability is MOST important for diagnosing this?

options.text: Model invocation logging of the final responses
options.why: Final responses alone do not show which reasoning step or tool call went wrong.

options.text: Agent observability: tracing each reasoning step and tool call
options.why: Step-by-step traces of reasoning, tool inputs and outputs show exactly where the workflow fails.

options.text: Bedrock Model Evaluation on a benchmark dataset
options.why: A benchmark score shows overall quality, not why this agent's specific runs fail.

options.text: CloudWatch alarms on the agent's error rate
options.why: Alarms tell you failures are happening, not which step causes them.

explanation.answer: Observability for agents means capturing traces of reasoning steps, tool invocations, parameters, results, latency and token usage. This lets teams pinpoint failures and measure quality and cost.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability provides tracing and metrics for agents, and Bedrock Agents exposes trace information for each step.
explanation.examTip: Need to see what the agent did step by step = observability / tracing.

stem: A company is choosing between a predefined workflow and an autonomous agent for two tasks. Task 1: generating a weekly report from the same three data sources in the same format. Task 2: researching open-ended customer questions that may need different sources and steps each time.
prompt: Which assignment is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Predefined workflow for both tasks
options.why: A fixed workflow cannot adapt to open-ended questions that need different steps each time.

options.text: Autonomous agent for both tasks
options.why: Using an agent for a fixed, repeatable task adds cost and unpredictability with no benefit.

options.text: Predefined workflow for Task 1 and autonomous agent for Task 2
options.why: Predictable, repeatable steps fit a deterministic workflow, while varied, open-ended tasks benefit from an agent's dynamic planning.

options.text: Autonomous agent for Task 1 and predefined workflow for Task 2
options.why: This is reversed. The predictable task suits a fixed workflow, and the variable task benefits from an agent's flexibility.

explanation.answer: Use deterministic workflows when steps are known and repeatable; they are cheaper, faster and more predictable. Use agents when the path to the goal varies and requires dynamic decisions about which tools and steps to use.
explanation.concept: Many production systems blend both: a fixed workflow that hands specific open-ended steps to an agent.
explanation.examTip: Known steps → workflow. Unknown or varying steps → agent.

stem: A team wants to connect its agent to a third-party MCP server it found online that offers file-management tools.
prompt: Which consideration is MOST important before connecting?

options.text: Whether the server's tools return results in JSON
options.why: Output format matters for integration, but the bigger risk is what an unvetted server can do with its access.

options.text: Whether the server supports the agent's framework
options.why: MCP is framework-independent; compatibility is not the main concern.

options.text: Whether the server meets the agent's latency budget
options.why: Performance matters less than whether the server can be trusted with file access.

options.text: Whether it is trustworthy and what access its tools would have
options.why: Tools can read data and take actions. An untrusted or over-privileged server could leak data or act harmfully, including through injected instructions.

explanation.answer: Connecting an agent to an MCP server gives the model the ability to use that server's tools. Teams should vet the server's provenance, restrict its permissions to the minimum needed, require authentication, validate inputs and outputs, and log tool calls.
explanation.concept: Tool outputs and descriptions can carry indirect prompt injection. Treat all external content as untrusted.
explanation.examTip: Third-party tools = verify trust, apply least privilege, log and monitor.

stem: A company is evaluating where AI agents could deliver the most value.
prompt: Which task is the BEST candidate for an AI agent?

options.text: Resolving refund requests: check orders, apply policy, issue refunds
options.why: This multi-step task needs reasoning, lookups and an action through an API, which is what agents are designed for.

options.text: Summarizing each support call transcript after it ends
options.why: Summarization is a single generation step; it does not need planning or actions in other systems.

options.text: Translating product pages into five languages
options.why: Translation is a single transformation task that a model or translation service handles without an agent.

options.text: Classifying incoming emails by department
options.why: Classification is a single prediction; a model or classifier handles it without planning or tool use.

explanation.answer: AI agents add the most value for multi-step tasks that require judgment, information gathering from several systems, and actions, such as customer service resolutions, IT support, research and back-office processing.
explanation.concept: Business value metrics for agents include task completion rate, time saved, cost per interaction and customer satisfaction.
explanation.examTip: Multi-step + judgment + actions in systems = good agent use case.

stem: A team wants to visually link prompts, a knowledge base, AWS Lambda functions and conditional logic into a reusable generative AI workflow on Amazon Bedrock, without managing orchestration code.
prompt: Which Amazon Bedrock capability fits this need?

options.text: Amazon Polly
options.why: Polly converts text to speech and is not a workflow builder.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Flows
options.why: Bedrock Flows lets you build generative AI workflows by connecting nodes such as prompts, knowledge bases, Lambda functions and conditions in a visual builder.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
options.why: Guardrails filter harmful content and sensitive information. They do not orchestrate workflows.

options.text: Provisioned Throughput
options.why: Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity. It does not define workflows.

explanation.answer: Amazon Bedrock Flows is a workflow builder for generative AI. You link nodes, such as prompts, models, knowledge bases, agents, Lambda functions, conditions and iterators, into a flow, version it and invoke it from applications.
explanation.concept: Flows suit predefined, repeatable generative AI workflows. Agents suit dynamic tasks in which the model decides the steps.
explanation.examTip: Visually connect prompts, knowledge bases and logic on Bedrock = Bedrock Flows.

stem: An agent has two tools named "get_data" and "fetch_info" with one-word descriptions. It frequently calls the wrong one.
prompt: Which change is MOST likely to improve the agent's tool selection?

options.text: Lower the temperature so tool choice is consistent
options.why: Consistent choices are not correct choices; the model still cannot tell the two tools apart.

options.text: Switch to a larger model with stronger reasoning
options.why: Even a strong model cannot reliably choose between two tools whose names and descriptions say nothing useful.

options.text: Give the tools distinct names and detailed descriptions and schemas
options.why: The model chooses tools from their names, descriptions and input schemas, so clear, distinct descriptions make the right choice obvious.

options.text: Merge both tools into one tool that does everything
options.why: A catch-all tool hides the difference rather than resolving it and makes inputs ambiguous.

explanation.answer: Foundation models decide which tool to call by reading the tool's name, description and input schema. Descriptive names, precise descriptions of purpose and usage, and well-defined parameters significantly improve tool selection.
explanation.concept: Tool design is part of context engineering: everything the model sees about tools affects its choices.
explanation.examTip: Agent picks wrong tool → improve tool names and descriptions.

references.title: Automate tasks with Amazon Bedrock Agents

stem: A company runs agents built by different vendors on different frameworks. It wants these agents to discover each other's capabilities and delegate tasks to one another, rather than each agent only calling tools.
prompt: Which statement BEST describes what is needed?

options.text: MCP servers for every agent's tools
options.why: MCP connects agents to tools and data; it does not let independent agents discover each other and delegate tasks.

options.text: A shared vector store that all agents read from
options.why: Shared data does not give agents a way to discover each other's capabilities or hand off tasks.

options.text: A supervisor agent built with one vendor's framework
options.why: A supervisor in one framework would still need a common protocol to talk to agents built on others.

options.text: An agent-to-agent protocol, complementing MCP for tools
options.why: Agent-to-agent protocols let agents describe capabilities and exchange tasks; MCP covers agent-to-tool connections.

explanation.answer: Multi-agent communication across frameworks needs a shared way to describe agent capabilities and exchange tasks. Agent-to-agent protocols (such as the open Agent2Agent protocol) address agent collaboration, while MCP addresses agent-to-tool connections. The two are complementary.
explanation.concept: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is framework-agnostic and supports hosting agents and tools that communicate through open protocols.
explanation.examTip: Agent ↔ tool = MCP. Agent ↔ agent = agent-to-agent protocol.

stem: A healthcare scheduling agent stores long-term memories about patients to personalize future conversations.
prompt: Which practice is MOST important for this memory design?

options.text: Minimize stored data, isolate it per user, encrypt it, set retention
options.why: Agent memory holds sensitive data, so minimization, per-user isolation, encryption and retention controls protect privacy.

options.text: Keep full transcripts for every patient to maximize personalization
options.why: Keeping everything increases privacy risk and cost and may break retention rules.

options.text: Store memories in the system prompt so every session has them
options.why: A system prompt is shared configuration; putting patient data there risks exposing it to others.

options.text: Share learned preferences across patients to improve defaults
options.why: Mixing memories across patients would leak private health information.

explanation.answer: Agent memory can contain personal and sensitive data. Good practice includes data minimization, strict separation by user or session, encryption at rest and in transit, access controls, and retention and deletion policies aligned with regulations.
explanation.concept: Managed memory services scope memories by identifiers such as actor and session, which supports isolation between users.
explanation.examTip: Agent memory = sensitive data → minimize, isolate, encrypt, set retention.
